subject: decomposing additive kernel functions in GP

messages.author: 91d53d643859f8d6
messages.subject: decomposing additive kernel functions in GP
parts:
Hi - 

I'm currently working on a GP-based poisson regression time-series model with a smooth component modeling a long-term trend (following a squared exponential kernel, k_s(x,x')) and a periodic component representing seasonality in disease incidence, i.e. k_p(x,x') = exp(-nu*sin^2(pi*(x-x'))), where nu is the frequency of the periodic component. So the covariance between two points is defined by k(x,x') = k_s(x,x') + k_p(x,x'). The data are reported as weekly counts over the course of about 7 years, and I assume that the periodic component has frequency 1/52.

This model is similar in spirit to the one that showed up on Andrew's blog for the birthday data a couple of years ago:

http://andrewgelman.com/2012/06/19/slick-time-series-decomposition-of-the-birthdays-data/

I'm wondering what the best way would be to then take a look at the rate ratios for each component, i.e. the long-term trend versus the seasonal components, as in the plots of the day of year, day of week, etc contributions in the birthday data blog post. 

Currently, for the seasonal component I'm planning on simulating from the GP posterior with the week of the year varying (i.e. from 1 to 52) and holding fixed the total number of weeks in the data, i.e. at 1. Would this be likely to yield the quantities I'm looking for? 

The other idea I had was to just break them apart into separate vars in the estimation, each with their own covariance, and then bring them back together  when evaluating the data likelihood, i.e. y_log_seasonal[t] + y_log_trend[t], but I was hoping to avoid doing this to keep the computational overhead down, and also wasn't sure if this would be equivalent to bringing them together in the covariance matrix.

Any ideas or suggestions would be greatly appreciated!

-Jon

messages.author: a236d3d356ca53fd
messages.subject: Re: decomposing additive kernel functions in GP
parts:
If f=f_1+f_2 and f_1~GP(mu_1,C_1), f_2~GP(mu_2,C_2) then f~GP(mu_1+mu_2,C_1+C2), so you can break them apart into separate vars.

For the composition, first consider Gaussian case with 
 y=f_1+f_2+e, where e~N(0,sigma^2)

When you want to look at the f_1 you can write
 y=f_1+e', where e'~N(mu_2+0,C_2+sigma^2)
and now you have divided the model to interesting signal f_1 and uninteresting correlated noise e'. Then you just use the usual prediction equations.

Correspondingly when you want to look at the f_2 you can write
 y=f_2+e', where e'~N(mu_1+0,C_1+sigma^2)
and now f_2 is the interesting signal.

For non-Gaussian models you just focus on the latent function
 f=f_1+f_2
but the conditioning that which part is signal and which is noise is handled in the same way.

I also recommend using product of periodic and squared exponential, so that the shape of the periodic component can change in time. This was used in birthdays example,see e.g how weekday effect changes in time.

I predict that in the future Stan will have better support for GPs, but meantime if you can install Octave, you might try GPstuff-toolbox, as it has all these implemented and much faster inference :)

Aki
